description:
We are passionate about technology, science, and space exploration. Our goal is to develop innovative solutions for astronaut health monitoring.

We are looking for creative, motivated people with skills in programming, UI/UX design, data science, AI, biology, medicine, or aerospace engineering.

You don't need to know everything — curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn are what matter most.

Join us and build something extraordinary!
summary:
We developed HeartVerse, an Astronaut Health Monitor that helps astronauts track and understand their health during long-duration space missions. The platform allows users to log in, record daily health indicators, view their overall health status at a glance, monitor trends over time, receive clear guidance on next steps, and generate reports for flight surgeons.
Because astronauts are not necessarily medical experts, every measurement includes simple instructions and explanations to support informed decision-making. Beyond displaying individual readings, the system analyzes combinations of mild symptoms and indicators to identify patterns associated with known spaceflight health risks. Each health metric is also connected to one of NASA’s recognized hazards of human spaceflight, helping users better understand potential threats to their well-being.
HeartVerse addresses the challenge of maintaining astronaut health in remote environments where immediate medical support is unavailable, promoting early detection, preventive care, and safer long-duration space exploration. As future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond become longer and more complex, reliable health monitoring and early risk detection are essential for astronaut safety, mission success, and sustainable human space exploration.
details:
Astronaut Health Monitor is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions track and understand their own health. On a trip to Mars, a message can take up to about 20 minutes to reach Earth, so crews can't count on real-time help from the ground. Each day, the astronaut records seven indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and resistance exercise. Every field explains how to take the measurement, and the astronaut reviews all values before saving so typos don't become false alarms. The app labels each reading as normal, attention or contact flight surgeon, and every status has a color, an icon and text. It also compares the reading with the astronaut's own baseline from their last 14 readings. It warns when several mild readings together match a known spaceflight risk, such as fatigue, infection or muscle and bone loss. Each indicator is linked to one of NASA's five official Human Research Program hazards and to a real countermeasure. The results appear on an interactive body map and on trend charts, with plain-language guidance, and the astronaut can export a CSV report for the flight surgeon.

The main benefit is self-reliance: astronauts with no medical training can understand their data and act on it early, while the ground team receives clear, organized information. We hope the app helps catch small health problems before they threaten a mission. The same approach could also serve people in isolated places on Earth, such as Antarctic stations or remote clinics.

We built it with JavaScript, React and Vite, used Recharts for the charts and drew the body map as inline SVG. The backend runs on Vercel serverless functions with a PostgreSQL database hosted on Neon, and passwords are hashed with scrypt. No special hardware is needed: the app runs in any browser, and the readings come from standard devices like a thermometer or a blood pressure cuff.

What makes the project creative is that it looks at patterns across indicators instead of judging one number at a time, and it measures each astronaut against their own normal rather than a generic one. It also explains why each value matters in space by tying it to NASA's own hazard framework. One-click demo scenarios load 14 days of data, so anyone can watch a health crisis unfold. Throughout development, the team focused on the communication delay, users without medical training, accessibility, scientific sources for every range and data security. We were also open about the app's limits: it is an educational prototype, not a medical device and not an official NASA product.
